vignette:
Joseph is a 65-year-old African man who works as a stock clerk at a large discount retail store. He arrived in the United States thirty years ago, and he still speaks with a soft, lilting accent that reminds his wife of the village where they grew up. Married for forty-two years, he has three grown children and four grandchildren. On the surface, his life appears settled—a small house with a garden, a steady job, a weekly card game with old friends. But since the flood, nothing is settled inside him.

The flood came two years ago, during a rainy season that was supposed to be mild. Joseph was at work when the storm surge hit his neighborhood. By the time he got home, the water was waist-deep in his street. He waded through the murky brown current, calling his wife’s name over the roar of the rain. She was safe—she had climbed onto the roof with the neighbor. But the neighbor, an elderly woman named Mama Esther, had slipped. Joseph saw her body float past him, her gray head bobbing against a broken fence. He grabbed her arm, but the current was too strong. She drifted away. He searched for hours until rescue workers pulled him away. They never found Mama Esther.

Now, every time it rains—even a light drizzle—Joseph’s chest tightens. He cancels plans, calls in sick, and sits in the darkest corner of his living room with the television off. His wife knows to leave him alone. “It’s just a little water,” she says gently, and he snaps, “You don’t know.” He apologizes later, but the shame lingers. He cannot explain why a passing shower makes him feel like he is drowning.

At work, Joseph has become quiet and jumpy. He used to chat with customers about their gardening projects, recommend the best bags of soil. Now he avoids the garden section altogether. When a child drops a soda bottle on the tile floor, the crack of plastic hitting concrete makes him drop what he is holding. His coworkers have noticed. “You okay, Joe?” they ask. He forces a smile and says he is just tired. He volunteers for the night restocking shifts, when the store is empty and the aisles are silent. He prefers the quiet. But even then, the hum of the fluorescent lights reminds him of the drone of rescue helicopters, and he finds himself standing frozen in the back room, staring at boxes of paper towels, unable to remember what he came for.

He sleeps poorly. He wakes at 3:00 a.m. with his heart hammering, convinced that water is creeping under the bedroom door. He checks the floorboards with a flashlight, then stands at the window, watching the street for rising water. His wife has learned to sleep on the couch when the nightmares are bad. Joseph does not tell her about the images that flash behind his eyelids: Mama Esther’s open eyes, the taste of muddy water, the sound of his own screams that he cannot stop.

He has stopped going to the weekly card game. The friends talk about their grandchildren, about vacations, about the weather. The weather. Someone mentions a forecast, and Joseph feels heat rise up his neck. He excuses himself to the bathroom and does not come back. He tells himself he will go next week, but he never does.

His wife brought home a small plant for the kitchen window. Joseph threw it in the trash. “It reminds me of the mud,” he said, and then he could not look at her. He knows he is changing, becoming someone cold and brittle. He wants to be himself again, but the self he remembers feels like a stranger. At sixty-five, he expected to feel tired. He did not expect to feel hunted.
